summary.text: A 39-year-old man with no known significant co-morbidities and not on antiretroviral therapy presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of shortness of breath and dry cough that had not improved with antibiotics for a lower respiratory tract infection. He was in severe respiratory distress with scattered bilateral predominantly basal crackles and an oxygen saturation of 62% on a partial rebreather mask.

Admission investigations showed a white cell count of 14.5 × 10^(9) cells/L, C-reactive protein of 102 mg/L, beta-d-glucan above 500 pg/mL, a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis on blood gas, diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates on chest X-ray and a normal echocardiogram. HIV testing was positive with a CD4 count of 7 cells/μL, and tuberculosis, bacterial and PCP antigen tests were negative. Pneumocystis pneumonia was considered clinically.

He was intubated, ventilated and admitted to the intensive care unit, and empirically started on piperacillin and tazobactam, a macrolide, high-dose intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and high-dose intravenous hydrocortisone. Lung protective ventilation, permissive hypoxaemia and meticulous fluid management were adopted, with ventilator settings weaned on day one of admission.

He was extubated on day four of admission and placed on non-invasive ventilation for a total of 3 days, then weaned onto oxygen supplementation with an FiO2 of 0.4. He was discharged to the ward on nasal cannula after a 7-day ICU stay, having been successfully weaned from mechanical ventilation.
